tagline: The northern half of a divided peninsula
overview:
North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, bordering China and Russia in the north and South Korea across a heavily fortified line in the south. It covers about 120,000 km², a little larger than Virginia, and mountains cover roughly four-fifths of it.

About 26 million people live in North Korea, all speaking Korean. Pyongyang, the capital, stands on the Taedong River and holds the country's grandest monuments, wide avenues and a subway decorated like a palace. Officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, it is a socialist state led since 1948 by three generations of one family: Kim Il Sung, Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un.

North Korea is one of the most closed and tightly controlled countries in the world. Travel inside the country, contact with foreigners, and access to outside news and the internet are strictly limited, and the state directs the economy and the media. It has developed nuclear weapons, which has led to international sanctions.
landAndNature: Steep forested mountains fill the north and east. Mount Paektu, an active volcano of 2,744 meters on the Chinese border, is the highest point on the peninsula and holds a deep crater lake called Heaven Lake in its summit. The Yalu and Tumen rivers mark the frontier with China. Narrow plains along the west coast, facing the Yellow Sea, grow most of the country's rice and corn; floods and droughts here have repeatedly caused food shortages. Winters are long and bitterly cold, with summer monsoon rains. The Demilitarized Zone dividing the two Koreas has been almost empty of people since 1953, and wildlife including rare cranes, black bears and possibly leopards has thrived in that four-kilometer-wide strip.
peopleAndCulture: Koreans on both sides of the border share a language, an alphabet called hangul, and a long culinary tradition of rice, kimchi, soups and grilled meat; naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, is a specialty of Pyongyang. North Korean life is organized around the state: schoolchildren learn the history of the ruling family, mass gymnastics displays fill stadiums with thousands of performers moving in unison, and giant statues and murals honor past leaders. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the women's national team has done well internationally. Taekwondo, which developed in Korea, is widely practiced. Most people live in apartment blocks in cities or in farming cooperatives, and private phones and computers are far less common than in neighboring countries.
history: Korea was a single country for more than a thousand years, ruled by the Goryeo and then Joseon dynasties, before Japan annexed it in 1910 and governed harshly until 1945. At the end of World War II the peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel: Soviet forces occupied the north, American forces the south. Two rival governments formed in 1948. In 1950 North Korea invaded the south, starting the Korean War; China entered on the north's side and a United Nations force led by the United States on the south's. Millions died and cities on both sides were flattened. The fighting stopped with an armistice in 1953, not a peace treaty, so the war has technically never ended. Kim Il Sung built a state around his own leadership, and his family has ruled since.
funFacts: North and South Korea have never signed a peace treaty, so the Korean War has formally paused rather than ended since 1953.
North Korea uses its own calendar in which year 1 is 1912, the birth year of Kim Il Sung.
The Demilitarized Zone between the Koreas is one of the most heavily guarded borders on Earth and an accidental wildlife refuge.
Pyongyang's metro stations sit more than 100 meters underground, among the deepest in the world.
North Korea and South Korea have marched together under one flag at some Olympic opening ceremonies.
